passage:
You want to know why I quit the late shifts, Akash? It's me, Thomas, the guy who used to code for fun on Sundays. Last year I was on three projects at once. Twelve-hour days for eight months.
My body started falling apart. I caught every cold going around. My back ached. I was tired even after sleeping. And the worst part: I stopped caring about the work. I used to love it. Now I'd stare at the code and feel nothing.
I took a two-week holiday in Goa. Came back, and within three days I felt exactly the same.
That's when I realised a holiday wasn't the fix. The load was. I told my manager I couldn't do three projects. We cut it to one. I stopped answering messages after seven, saw my doctor about the colds, and started sleeping properly.
It's taken months. But last Sunday I opened my laptop and wrote something just for fun again.

qa.q: How many projects was Thomas on last year?
qa.a: Thomas was on three projects at once.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel about the work once loved so much?
qa.a: Thomas felt detached and empty, staring at the code and feeling nothing.

qa.q: What did Thomas realise after the holiday, and what changed?
qa.a: Thomas realised the load, not the lack of a holiday, was the problem, so the projects were cut to one, evening limits were set, a doctor was seen and sleep improved.

qa.q: How might Thomas's manager have felt on hearing that three projects were too many?
qa.a: The manager may have been surprised at first, but agreed to cut it to one, suggesting they valued Thomas staying well.

grounding: It shows a worker in long-term overload with tiredness, colds, aches and detachment, and how cutting the workload and resting helps more than a holiday.

passage:
I'm Pema. I teach at the same school as Kalyani, and I've shared the staff room with her for three years.
Kalyani used to be the loudest laugh in there. She ran the science club and stayed late to help students with projects. This year she took on exam duty, two extra classes and the annual day.
By December she always seemed to have a cold. She'd rub her lower back and sit with her eyes closed at lunch. When students came with project questions, she answered politely but flatly.
After the winter break she came back looking the same, pale and tired.
In January I saw her go into the principal's office. Afterwards her name was off the annual day list and one of the extra classes. I don't know everything she said. But last week she laughed in the staff room again, and it sounded like her.

qa.q: What extra work did Kalyani take on this year?
qa.a: She took on exam duty, two extra classes and the annual day.

qa.q: What might Kalyani have been feeling by December?
qa.a: She may have been exhausted and detached, though Pema can't be sure; she seemed tired, often ill and flat with students.

qa.q: What change seems to have helped Kalyani most?
qa.a: Talking to the principal and dropping the annual day and an extra class, since the break alone had not helped.

qa.q: How might Kalyani's students have experienced her in December?
qa.a: They probably noticed she was polite but flat, and may have missed her old warmth and energy.

grounding: It shows, through a colleague's eyes, a teacher in long-term overload with colds, aches and detachment, who recovers after her workload is reduced rather than only after a holiday.

passage:
Dear Ramesh,
I'm writing because I don't think I can say this properly in a meeting.
For the past eight months, I've been doing two people's jobs since Arjun left. I've had four colds this year. My back aches all the time, and I'm tired even after a full night's sleep. Worst, I've stopped caring about work I used to love. I sit at my desk and feel nothing.
I took a week's holiday in March, thinking it would fix this. It didn't. Two days back and I felt exactly the same.
I think my body is telling me the workload needs to change, not just that I need a break. Could we talk about hiring for Arjun's role or moving some projects? I want to keep doing good work here.
Sharmila

qa.q: How many colds has Sharmila had this year?
qa.a: Four colds.

qa.q: How does Sharmila feel about work now?
qa.a: Sharmila feels detached and exhausted, feeling nothing about work once loved.

qa.q: What does Sharmila ask for, and why?
qa.a: A change in workload through hiring or moving projects, because a holiday did not fix the exhaustion.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Ramesh may be concerned and perhaps guilty, realising how long Sharmila has carried two jobs.

grounding: Shows a worker in long-term overload feeling tired, catching colds, aching and detached, and asking for a change in workload rather than only a holiday.

passage: Harsha, you keep asking why I quit the startup. Okay. It's Pankaj, let me tell you honestly. For a year I worked twelve-hour days. At first I loved it. Then I started getting sick every month: colds, fevers, a bad back. I was always tired, even after sleeping ten hours on Sunday. Worst of all, I stopped caring. The product I'd been so proud of? I felt nothing when it launched. I took a week in Goa, thinking I just needed a break. Came back and within two days, same exhaustion. That's when I got it: my body wasn't asking for a holiday. It was asking for a different life. I talked to my manager about cutting my hours. When that didn't happen, I left. Now I'm at a smaller company, sleeping properly. Haven't had a cold in months.

qa.q: Where did Pankaj go for a week's break?
qa.a: To Goa.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel when the product launched?
qa.a: Pankaj felt nothing, detached from work once loved.

qa.q: What did Pankaj realise about the holiday?
qa.a: That a holiday could not fix exhaustion from constant overload; the body was asking for a real change in workload.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel hearing the full story?
qa.a: Harsha may feel surprised and more understanding of why Pankaj left.

grounding: Shows a worker in long-term overload with tiredness, frequent illness, aches and detachment, realising the body is asking for a workload change, not just a holiday.

passage:
January: Reena, twenty-five, had her third cold since Diwali. She was tired all the time and her shoulders ached, but deadlines kept coming.
March: She took a week off to the hills. On the first day back, she sat at her desk and felt nothing at all about the campaign she used to love. The exhaustion was back by Wednesday.
May: Reena saw her doctor, who found nothing seriously wrong but asked about her hours. Then she asked her manager, Chinmay, for a meeting. 'I'm not okay. I've been overloaded for a year.' Chinmay listened. They moved two accounts to a colleague and agreed she'd leave by six. By July, Reena had stopped catching colds, and one afternoon she laughed at a campaign idea, surprised to find she cared again.

qa.q: Where did Reena go in March?
qa.a: To the hills.

qa.q: How did Reena feel on her first day back in March?
qa.a: She felt empty and detached, feeling nothing about the campaign she used to love.

qa.q: What changes helped Reena recover?
qa.a: A doctor's check, telling Chinmay honestly, moving two accounts and leaving by six.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt hearing Reena say she was not okay?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and concerned, and wanted to help reduce her load.

grounding: Shows a worker in long-term overload with tiredness, frequent colds, aches and detachment, whose body needs a lasting workload change rather than only a holiday.

passage: Bidisha, you remind me of myself at twenty-five, so let your old boss Rajni tell you a story. I was in audit then, and I said yes to everything. For two years I caught every cold that went round the office, my back ached as if I'd carried bricks, and I slept ten hours on Sundays and still woke up tired. Worse, I stopped caring. Files I used to love felt like grey sand. Everyone said, "Take a holiday." So I went to Goa for a week, came back, and by Wednesday I was exactly where I'd started. The turning point was a doctor who asked, "What will change in your work when you go back?" Nothing, I said. So I went to my manager and gave up two clients. That's when my body started to recover. So, Bidisha. What will change in yours?

qa.q: Where did Rajni go on holiday?
qa.a: To Goa, for a week.

qa.q: How did young Rajni feel about the audit files after two years of overload?
qa.a: Rajni felt detached and drained; files Rajni used to love felt like grey sand.

qa.q: What turning point in the story led to real recovery?
qa.a: The doctor's question made Rajni see nothing would change, so Rajni asked the manager to cut the load by two clients.

qa.q: How might Rajni's manager have seen the request to give up two clients?
qa.a: The manager may have been surprised, but the request gave an honest picture of an overloaded employee.

grounding: Illustrates a worker in long-term overload with constant tiredness, frequent colds, aches and detachment, whose body needed a change in workload rather than only a holiday.
